messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin was six years old in the winter of 1944 when the bombs fell on his small German town. He was in the back seat of his father’s car, wedged between suitcases, as they tried to flee toward the countryside. A low-flying plane roared overhead, and then the world turned white and silent. When he came to, the car was on its side, his mother was not moving, and his father’s hand hung limp through the shattered windshield. He lay there for hours, pinned and bleeding, listening to the crackle of fires and the distant drone of engines. That night became the fixed point around which the rest of his life would orbit. When he recalls it now—and he does, often—it comes not as a story but as a series of images: the grey sky through the broken window, the smell of gasoline, the weight of the suitcase pressing into his ribs. Sometimes he feels like he is still in that car. Other times he can describe every detail but feels nothing at all, as if it happened to a stranger.

After the war, Martin was placed in an orphanage in the United States with a sponsor family. He never spoke of what he saw. But he carried it. He came to believe, quietly and without argument, that the world was a place where safety could vanish without warning. That belief—that the world is dangerous—was not just an idea; it shaped the way his memory worked. When he felt particularly certain that danger was near, the images of the car and his parents would return more vividly, more insistently, as if his mind was reminding him that this was how things really were. And each time those images came back, his conviction deepened. He would think, *See, this is what I mean. You cannot trust anything*. Memory and appraisal locked into a tightening circuit.

As an adult, Martin became a cashier at a grocery store—a job that kept him indoors, behind a counter, where he could see everyone who entered. It was a position he chose partly because he could no longer drive, and partly because it allowed him to watch. He started scanning customers’ faces as soon as they walked through the door, looking for anyone who moved too quickly, who seemed agitated, who might be carrying something. This vigilance was exhausting, but it felt necessary. When a memory of the war surfaced—a sudden flash of the overturned car while he was ringing up bread—he would startle and then watch the customer even more closely, certain that the memory was a warning. That vigilance, in turn, kept the belief alive: if he had to be on guard, the world must indeed be dangerous.

The same memories drove him to avoid. He had never learned to drive, but he also refused to be a passenger in any vehicle. He walked to work, rain or snow, two miles each way. When coworkers offered him a ride, he refused, sometimes brusquely, because the thought of being trapped in a car with no control made his chest tighten. That avoidance reinforced his sense of himself as diminished—*I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me*, he would think, though he never said it aloud. He also pushed away positive feelings. When a customer smiled at him or a child laughed near his register, he felt a flutter of warmth, but he quickly suppressed it. Positive emotions felt unsafe, as if they invited catastrophe. He had decided, somewhere along the way, that feeling good was a kind of vulnerability, a lowering of his guard. So he stayed flat, watchful, and the avoidance of joy only made the world seem more threatening. But that very avoidance — of joy, of connection, of ever revisiting the past — had the unintended effect of keeping the memory of the car and his parents exactly where it was: untouched, unexamined, and ready to surge back the instant his guard slipped.

At night, Martin struggled to fall asleep. He had to stay alert, he felt, scanning the shadows of his bedroom. This sleep vigilance was a constant companion. It was tied to the memories: on nights when the reliving was strongest, he would lie awake for hours, listening. And his avoidance—his refusal to let himself relax or feel safe—fed back into the vigilance, because he never practised the skill of letting go.

Now, at seventy-six, widowed and living alone, Martin has spent decades in this loop. He continues to work, because the routine holds him together, but he no longer enjoys it. He thinks often about why the event happened to him—why he survived and not his parents—and the question never yields an answer, only a dull ache of lost faith in people, in life, in God. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning last month when he stood at the curb outside the grocery store, unable to cross the street because a delivery truck was idling at the corner. He stood there for fifteen minutes, heart pounding, images of the wrecked car flooding in, and when he finally made it inside, he realised he could not keep living like this. He is afraid that talking about it will make it worse, but he is more afraid of one day standing frozen and never moving again.
